# UK Government Analysis Function, the AQuA Book (2025 edition): quality assurance of analysis for government

**Source:** UK Government Analysis Function. *The AQuA Book* (the Analytical Quality Assurance Book), 2025 edition, GOV.UK guidance, https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-aqua-book ; first published 2025-07-30 per the operator's source record, which lists the Government Operational Research Service, the Government Actuary's Department and the Office for National Statistics as co-publishers. No single author; the revised edition was produced by a task and finish group of fourteen named members. Open Government Licence v3.0; contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0; this reference paraphrases and quotes the source.
**Scope:** open
**Structure:** a single guidance page: acknowledgements, ten numbered chapters (definitions and themes in 1 to 5; the four life-cycle stages in 6 to 9, each in the same internal order; resources in 10) and a closing "Improving the book". Cited as `(Ch N, "Section heading")`.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The AQuA Book is UK government guidance on "producing good quality analysis for government to support well informed decision-making that creates better outcomes and improve the lives of citizens" [V] (Ch 1, "Introduction"). It holds that no single piece of guidance can say whether analysis is good enough for its purpose, and offers principles instead: assurance proportionate to the risk of the intended use and the complexity of the method, assurance throughout the life cycle, both verification (error-free and to specification) and validation (fit for its purpose), and acceptance that uncertainty is inherent in every input and output (Ch 1, "Principles of analytical quality assurance"). The 2025 edition updates the 2015 book for open-source software, machine learning and AI, and adds guidance on multi-use models, black box systems, maintenance and continuous review, third parties and publishing models (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)").

Its few hard requirements are written as "shall": "All analysis shall be assured." [V], and "The assurer and the analyst shall be independent." [V], with the level of assurance guided by a structured assessment of business risk, meaning the potential effect of an error combined with its likelihood (Ch 3, "Proportionality"; "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"). Four roles (commissioner, analyst, assurer, approver) carry responsibilities through four stages (engagement and scoping; design; analysis; delivery, communication and sign-off), in a cycle that is often iterative (Ch 5). Around this it argues that a quality assurance culture, led and resourced by senior leaders, open about errors and transparent with the public, is vital (Ch 4; Ch 9, "9.7 Analytical transparency").

## Purpose, audience and the modal verbs

The book is the supporting guide to the Government Functional Standard for Analysis, which says its guidance "should be followed" [V] [BT], and is referred to by the Green Book, the Magenta Book, the Duck Book and an NAO guide for audit committees (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)"). It is written for "anyone who commissions, uses, conducts, or assures analysis" [V] in government, and says the guidance is broadly applicable beyond it (Ch 1, "1.2 Who the AQuA Book is for"). Its aims include minimising "the risk of errors arising that cause operational, business or reputational damage" [V], building trust, handling changing requirements and re-use, and supporting audit (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book").

It defines its modal verbs, consistent with the UK Government Functional Standards: "shall" is a mandatory requirement applying in all circumstances; "should" is a recommendation "to be met on a ‘comply or explain’ basis" [V]; "may" is a good idea but neither mandatory nor advisory; "might" a possibility; "can" capability and possibility (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book"). The text also uses "must", which the list does not define. The life-cycle figure is described as often iterative, with stages that "may repeat or happen out of order" [V], and proportionality considered at every stage (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book").

## Principles and RIGOUR

"Quality assurance effort should be appropriate to the risk associated with the intended use of the analysis and the complexity of the analytical approach." [V] (Ch 1, "1.3.1 Proportionate assurance"). Assurance should run through the whole life cycle (1.3.2). It is "more than checking that the analysis is error-free and satisfies its specification (verification)" [V]; it should also check fitness for purpose (validation) (1.3.3). Uncertainty is inherent in all analysis and is treated stage by stage (1.3.4).

RIGOUR is offered as questions analysts ask of their own work: Repeatable (if repeated, "the results should be as expected" [V], though exact matches are not guaranteed), Independent (as far as possible free of prejudice or bias), Grounded in reality, Objective (engagement and suitable challenge reduce bias), Uncertainty-managed, and Robust (error free in the context of residual uncertainty and accepted limitations) (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").

## Definitions and the documentation set

"Analytical assurance is the process and set of practices that ensure analysis is fit for purpose." [V] (Ch 2, "Assurance"). Black box models are those whose internal workings are not visible, easily understood or succinctly explained, including proprietary models; "AI models are usually considered black box models" [V] (Ch 2, "Artificial Intelligence"; "Black box models"). Business critical analysis significantly influences finance or operations, is necessary to a departmental business plan, or could cause significant reputational, economic or legal damage if wrong (Ch 2, "Business critical analysis"). "Quality analysis is fit for the purpose it was commissioned to meet." [V] (Ch 2, "Quality analysis"). Verification checks the analysis against its design requirements; validation checks it meets users' needs in the intended use environment (Ch 2, "Validation"; "Verification").

The documentation set: a specification (question, context, boundaries, constraints and the required level of assurance); a design document (plan and planned verification and validation); assumptions, decisions and data logs recording what, when, why, who made and who signed off; user and technical documentation, which all analysis "shall have" [V] even if the only user is the analyst; and an assurance statement describing the assurance done and its known limitations (Ch 2, "Documentation"). Version control lets the latest version be used and changes be seen and assured (Ch 2, "Version control").

## Proportionality

All analysis shall be assured; the assurer and analyst shall be independent, with the degree of separation depending on importance, size and complexity; the analyst should still assure their own work, and "there shall also be some formal independent assurance" [V] (Ch 3, "Proportionality"). Table 3-1 lists ten factors for setting the level: business criticality, the analysis's weight in the decision, type and complexity, novelty (confidence grows as a technique is repeatedly tested), reuse or repurposing (which may need fresh verification and validation), required precision, resource (value for money "must be balanced" against benefits and risk appetite), longevity ("robust change control and regular review" [V]), effects on the public, and repeat runs (concentrate on version control and each run's data and parameters) (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance"). Figure 3-1 scales four interventions with risk and complexity: consultation on methods, use of RAP tools, analyst-assurer separation (from analyst-led testing to external audit) and documentation detail; they "must not be viewed in isolation" [V] and should build on each other (Ch 3, "3.1").

Business risk is effect times likelihood; "In situations where the risk is high, it is more important to reduce likelihood of errors than the level of the effect." [V], since the effect is usually beyond the analyst's control (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"). Table 3-3 sets responses: "High risk should not be tolerated." [V] (new assurance measures must be considered, else terminate or transfer the risk, else the commissioner should fully understand it); "Medium risk should not be tolerated without the agreement of the commissioner." [V]; low and very low risk can be tolerated. Under time pressure, "addressing the areas of greatest risk should take priority" [V] and the commissioner should be told what risks remain (Ch 3, "3.2"). Externally commissioned work and black-box models get the same structured approach (Ch 3, "3.3"; "3.4").

## Quality assurance culture

"A strong quality assurance culture starts with senior leaders." [V], who are accountable for analytical quality, should empower everyone to raise concerns at any level, and should build processes for reporting when things go wrong, reviewing failures in the assurance process and sharing lessons (Ch 4, "4.1 Leadership"). A box describes the Department for Education's internal and published external review after an error in its 2024-25 schools funding allocations [AE] (Ch 4, "An open culture when things go wrong").

Under time pressure, "If time constraints mean insufficient assurance has taken place this should be explicitly acknowledged and reported in an assurance statement that sets out the known limitations and conditions associated with the analysis." [V]; "Peer review should be carried out by independent, skilled and competent individuals or groups." [V] (Ch 4, "4.2.1 Capacity"). The chapter covers capability, quality assurance champions, tools, data, uncertainty (decision makers should challenge analysts on it), governance ("Each organisation should have a defined and established approach to assurance." [V]), transparency, and third parties, where the commissioning department remains accountable (Ch 4, "4.2.2" to "4.8").

## Roles and the analytical lifecycle

Each role may be filled by a team, but "a single individual (for example, the chair of a committee) will have overall accountability for each role" [V]. The commissioner requests, agrees and accepts the work; the analyst designs and does the analysis and their own assurance and acts on the assurer's findings; the assurer reviews that assurance, does further verification and validation, reports errors, re-reviews and confirms to the approver, and "must be independent from the analysts" [V]; the approver scrutinises and confirms the work was appropriately assured (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities"). One person may hold several roles on quick or simple work, "apart from the assurer and analyst roles which shall be separate from one another in all cases" [V] (Ch 5, "5.1").

All projects involve every phase in some form; in analysis, "traceable documentation of the assurance activities that have been undertaken shall also be produced" [V]; sign-off formally approves results for dissemination and may be phased (Ch 5, "5.2" to "5.2.4"). "The analytical lifecycle is not a linear process." [V]: analysis in ongoing use should be regularly re-checked (inputs, communication, supported software, calibration), under robust version control (Ch 5, "5.3 Maintenance and continuous review"). Urgent analysis may not follow every step when "the need for the analysis may outweigh the risk of poor quality" [V] (Ch 5, "5.4 Urgent analysis").

## Engagement and scoping

Commissioner and analyst shape the work "by developing a shared understanding of the problem and the context" [V] (Ch 6, "Engagement and scoping"). The analyst writes a specification capturing question, context, boundaries, constraints, assumptions, risks, uncertainties and business-criticality; "It should state the acceptable level of risk and the required level of assurance." [V]; the commissioner signs it off and the assurer may confirm it captures the engagement (Ch 6, "6.1.1" to "6.1.4"). The stage should agree outputs "including acceptable levels of accuracy, precision and margins of error" [V], and the specification becomes the reference for later validation and the approver's evidence at delivery (Ch 6, "6.2 Assurance activities"; "6.3 Documentation").

Ill-defined problems may need problem structuring methods (Strategic Choice Approach, Rich Pictures, Systems Thinking) [BT] (Ch 6, "6.2"). Where black box models such as AI are to be delivered, scoping "should include discussions around ethics and risks to assess whether such models would be appropriate for addressing the given problem" [V], covering regulation, skills, governance, regular tests that the model still works, and risk management (Ch 6, "6.5 Black box models").

## Design

The analyst turns the scope into an analytical plan covering methodology, version control, code management and testing, verification and validation, documentation, ongoing review and maintenance, and ethics; "Iteration of the plan between the commissioner and the analyst is normal and expected" [V] (Ch 7, "Design"). Reproducible analytical pipelines are the recommended approach for analysis in code, and shall follow the Duck Book's practices and the RAP minimum viable product [BT] (Ch 7, "Reproducible analytical pipelines"). The assurer reviews the plan, and design assurance asks whether it will meet requirements (validation), deliver as intended (verification) and meet RIGOUR, for complex work "ideally with tests baselining their response against independent reference cases" [V] (Ch 7, "7.1.3"; "7.2 Assurance activities").

"Using black box models places greater weight on the design of the analysis and the assurance and validation of outputs by domain experts." [V] (Ch 7, "7.5 Black box models"). For AI and machine learning the plan should cover data quality, a training, validation and test split, testing of pre-trained models, automatic checks that flag unexpected behaviour, retraining thresholds, ethics referral and peer review (Ch 7, "7.5"). Multi-use models should assure "both the assurance of individual modules and their integration" [V] (Ch 7, "7.6 Multi-use models").

## Analysis

The planned analysis is done and assured, with "appropriate and traceable records of the analysis and assurance activities conducted, changes, decisions and assumptions made" [V] (Ch 8, "Analysis"). "The analyst has primary responsibility for conducting verification and validation." [V]; "The assurer shall:" [V] review the analyst's assurance, carry out further verification and validation, report errors and review code practice, and should consider whether they are qualified to assure a revised method (Ch 8, "8.1.3"; "8.2.1 Verification and validation"). The book passes on six classes of verification technique from Whitener and Balci (1989) [BT]: informal, static, dynamic, symbolic, constraint and formal; validation tests whether the product meets users' requirements and should involve them (Ch 8, "8.2.1").

Data validity is "a vital part of analysis" [V], and data may carry a sunset date (Ch 8, "8.2.2 Data validity and data considerations"). "The analyst shall follow the guidance for good quality code development in a proportionate manner and the assurer shall review this accordingly." [V] (Ch 8, "8.2.3 Assurance of code"). Black box assurance should include the design-stage verification and verification of automatic tests that the model behaves as expected, and may include live performance testing; multi-use models can assure integration "by using test suites" [V] (Ch 8, "8.5 Black box models"; "8.6 Multi-use models").

## Delivery, communication and sign-off

Delivery marks the analysis's transition "from being a product under development to one that is fit and ready to be used" [V] (Ch 9, "Delivery, communication and sign-off"). The approver shall review the assurance evidence, be confident the analysis meets the design requirements and is of sufficient quality and proportionately documented, and follow governance for sign-off; the assurer (or analyst) communicates the assurance state, including that the work was scoped, executed, validated, verified and documented (Ch 9, "9.1.3"; "9.1.4"). Delivery evidence may include provision for regular review or a "sunset date", "a date beyond which the analysis and / or the model should not be used" [V], a risk assessment, and a completed assurance statement (Ch 9, "9.2.1 Delivery"). Sign-off formality should be proportionate, and the approver should give the analyst evidence of formal approval (Ch 9, "9.2.3 Sign-off").

Handover documentation includes specification and design, logs, user and technical documentation, the limits of use, change and version control logs and error reporting, the test plan and test results, and a statement of assurance (Ch 9, "9.3 Documentation"). The approver signs off that black-box risks and ethics have been addressed and model "health" is reported regularly, since "Model effectiveness can change over time." [V] through data drift (Ch 9, "9.5"; "Regularly reviewing model health"). Multi-use models carry a greater risk of use outside their intended scope (Ch 9, "9.6"), and departments should publish a business critical models register "at least annually" [V] (Ch 9, "9.7.1").

## Key Connections

- Government Functional Standard for Analysis: the book is its supporting guide; the life-cycle figure is adapted from it [BT].
- The Duck Book (*Quality Assurance of Code for Analysis and Research*): the code practices analysts shall follow proportionately and assurers review; RAPs shall follow it [BT].
- The Green, Magenta and Orange Books, *Managing Public Money* Annex 4.2, and NAO guidance on model review and uncertainty [BT].
- The Uncertainty Toolkit for Analysts in Government, used across every stage [BT].
- Government AI assurance guidance (Generative AI Framework for HMG, *Introduction to AI assurance*, the AI Playbook, the Data Ethics Framework) for black-box models [BT].
- Whitener and Balci (1989) for verification techniques; Paul Glover's note on verification and validation [BT].
- Departmental examples: DfE's Maturity Model and funding-formula review, HMRC's review team and champions network, DESNZ's QA colleges, and the Government Actuary's Department as an external reviewer [AE].

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Assurance is more than verification: checking against the specification is not enough without validation of fitness for purpose.
2. Independence does not stop the analyst assuring their own work; it adds formal independent assurance on top.
3. Assuring simple, low-influence analysis for months is out of proportion.
4. The Figure 3-1 interventions do not stand alone: high-risk work also uses the low-risk methods.
5. The analytical lifecycle is not linear.
6. Where risk is high, reducing the likelihood of errors matters more than reducing their effect.
7. The analyst and assurer roles are never combined, even on quick or simple work.
